Learning to Design SR Solvers: Harness Optimization for Symbolic Regression

Qian Li Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo, China Email: qianl01205@sjtu.edu.cn    Yuxiao Hu Affiliation: Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo, China Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China Email: yuxiao.hu@connect.polyu.hk    Qihao Duan Affiliation: Epigenetics Laboratory, Max Planck Institute for Heart and Lung Research    Jinyue Yan Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China    Yuntian Chen ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo, China
Abstract

Symbolic regression (SR) seeks explicit equations that explain observed data, and recent methods increasingly employ large language models (LLMs) and agents for equation discovery. However, these systems typically rely on manually designed workflows and prompts. We argue that the SR agent harness should itself be an optimization target: its design shapes search priors and how numerical feedback guides subsequent equation refinement. We therefore propose HarnessSR, a framework for jointly optimizing prompts and workflows to construct reusable SR agents. During both harness optimization and agent execution, HarnessSR supports either PySR or an LLM-based equation generator through tool-specific interfaces, allowing the framework to optimize search guidance for different equation-discovery mechanisms. HarnessSR first optimizes role prompts through equation-discovery feedback in basic workflows, then jointly searches prompt assignments and workflows with brief adaptation to align the two. Finally, it refines role instructions through reflection on residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes, improving how these signals guide subsequent equation search. On LSR-Synth in LLM-SRBench, HarnessSR achieves a mean ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} of 61.33% across three backbones, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline.

1 Introduction

Symbolic regression (SR) seeks explicit mathematical relationships that explain observed data (Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b; Karniadakis et al., 2021; Krenn et al., 2022; Udrescu and Tegmark, 2020; Udrescu et al., 2020). The resulting equations can be inspected, interpreted, and manipulated, and related to conservation laws, dimensional constraints, and domain theories. SR thus goes beyond numerical prediction to turn observations into testable scientific hypotheses, supporting equation discovery across physics, biology, materials science, and other domains.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agents have introduced a new paradigm for SR. These methods combine the scientific knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs with numerical search, evaluation, and feedback to iteratively propose, test, and revise equation hypotheses (Xia et al., 2025; Shojaee et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Central to these systems is the solver harness: the executable layer of role instructions, tool interfaces, and control logic that governs interactions between the LLM, data, and numerical tools. The harness governs how scientific knowledge informs candidate proposals and how numerical feedback guides decisions to retain, revise, or replace them. These decisions shape whether subsequent computation explores alternative functional forms, addresses structural errors, or repeats attempts, thereby affecting the quality of equations recovered within a given budget.

However, recent SR solver largely focus on designing solver harnesses by hand, rather than treating the solver harness itself as an object of systematic optimization. Recent research shows that, even with the base model fixed, harness choices can affect both task performance and inference resource use (Lee et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). Solver harness optimization extends beyond adding new SR roles. Within a fixed workflow, different instructions and few-shot demonstrations can shift the model’s output distribution. Conversely, with SR roles and prompts held fixed, changes in workflow topology—including invocation frequency and parallelism—can alter information flow, computational allocation, and final outcomes. These choices influence how data analysis informs equation search, how fitting and residual feedback guide candidate revision, and how finite computation is allocated between exploration and refinement. The SR agent harness is therefore not merely an execution scaffold, but a design variable to be optimized for equation discovery. This motivates us to develop a method for automatically optimizing the harness for reusable SR agent, aiming to improve both the quality and efficiency of equation discovery.

To this end, we introduce HarnessSR, a framework for optimizing reusable SR solver harnesses. We formulate harness design as the joint optimization of role instructions, demonstrations, and workflow organization to obtain an SR agent harness capable of discovering higher-quality equations. To address the strong coupling among these components and tailor their behavior to SR, we adopt a three-stage procedure. First, we optimize role prompts within basic workflows to establish strong starting points for joint search. Second, we jointly optimize workflows and prompt assignments, with brief adaptation to accommodate their interdependence. Third, we use a reflection model to diagnose failures in SR execution traces and refine role instructions, enabling the harness to translate residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes into targeted search guidance. This guidance is applied through tool-specific interfaces that translate agent-generated search plans into parameters and inputs for two selectable base SR tools (we integrates PySR and an LLM-based equation generator as agent tools). These interfaces allow agents to steer the chosen tool during both harness optimization and deployment, while keeping its underlying search algorithm fixed. The top-performing harness is then frozen and reused across new SR tasks, with model weights and the underlying search algorithms held fixed. Across three backbones on LSR-Synth, HarnessSR achieves a mean ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} of 61.33%, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline.

Our main contributions are: (1) We highlight that the solver agent harness can also be regarded as an optimization target for SR task. Its design shapes the LLM’s reasoning process, influencing the priors that guide equation search, how search feedback is interpreted and used, and ultimately the quality of the discovered equations. (2) We propose HarnessSR, an SR agent optimization framework that jointly optimizes prompts and workflows and uses reflection on SR execution traces to adapt harness behavior to equation discovery. (3) We demonstrate a 45.0% relative improvement in mean ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} over the next-best baseline across three backbones on LSR-Synth.

2 Related Work

Symbolic Regression.   Classical SR methods include genetic programming, which evolves expressions through crossover, and mutation (Koza, 1994; Stephens, 2024; Pawlak and Krawiec, 2018; Moraglio et al., 2012; de Franca and Aldeia, 2021). PySR combines evolutionary search with expression simplification and constant optimization (Cranmer, 2023). Neural-guided methods such as DSR learn a distribution over expressions using a recurrent neural network and guide candidate generation through risk-seeking policy gradients (Petersen et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025a; Li et al., ; Meidani et al., 2023; Kamienny et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022; Shojaee et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2025).

LLM-based methods leverage the generative capacity, prior knowledge, and reasoning capabilities of LLMs to guide equation search. LLM-SR and SGA couple LLM-generated structural hypotheses with numerical parameter optimization (Shojaee et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2024). Beyond candidate generation, LaSR introduces a learned concept library to guide evolutionary search (Grayeli et al., 2024), while RESTART uses residual feedback to guide an LLM in revising candidate equation structures (Li and Pan, 2026). Deliberate Evolution guides LLM-based equation generation with adaptive search operators, structural diagnostics, and reflective memory (Pang et al., 2026).

Agentic methods extend this paradigm through tool use and feedback-driven interaction. SR-Scientist autonomously invokes data-analysis and equation-evaluation tools to refine hypotheses (Xia et al., 2025). KeplerAgent extracts physical properties, including symmetries, to configure numerical SR engines Yang et al. (2026). A-SR introduces hierarchical coordination to adapt role selection, memory use, and feedback routing during search (Zhao et al., 2026).

Despite increasingly autonomous execution, the overarching harness in representative SR systems remains largely hand-designed. For example, SR-Scientist selects tools autonomously, but does so within predefined tool interfaces, instruction templates, and outer-loop control rules. Such autonomy adapts the search within a given harness without optimizing the harness itself. Yet these design choices govern how hypotheses are proposed and how evidence guides subsequent search, making them integral to the equation-discovery strategy. Therefore, we focus on optimizing the solver harness under a limited budget to obtain stronger, reusable SR solvers.

Self-Evolving Agents. Self-evolution and automated agent design extend optimization from individual outputs to the procedures that produce them. MIPRO optimizes instructions and demonstrations using end-to-end task feedback (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024). MASS optimizes prompts for individual building blocks, selects how these blocks are composed, and then refines their prompts within the selected workflow (Zhou et al., 2026), while Meta-Harness searches executable code surrounding a fixed language model using execution feedback (Lee et al., 2026). However, existing methods have devoted limited attention to harness optimization for automated scientific discovery. In our paper, we show that optimizing the solver harness can substantially improve both the quality and efficiency of scientific discovery.

3 Method

Unlike prior SR methods that manually design a new solver, we optimize the solver harness itself. For an SR agent, HarnessSR jointly searches role prompts, activation, parallelism, and iteration. To coordinate these coupled components for equation discovery, we adopt a three-stage procedure. The resulting top-performing SR agent is reusable and better coordinates scientific reasoning with numerical search under limited compute.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Given an SR task qq, typically comprising scientific context, variable descriptions, and observed data, an SR agent SS seeks an explicit equation explaining the observations. With the base language model MM fixed, SS is instantiated from its harness ℋ\mathcal{H} and returns f^q\hat{f}_{q}:

S=Instantiate⁡(M,ℋ),f^q=S⁡(q).S=\operatorname{Instantiate}(M,\mathcal{H}),\qquad\hat{f}_{q}=S(q).

We aim to optimize SR agents by optimizing their harnesses without changing the LLM weights.

We define ℋ=(ℛ,w,ℱ)\mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{R},w,\mathcal{F}), where ℛ\mathcal{R} specifies the typical roles in SR agent and their prompts:

ℛ={(r,Pr)|r∈{Planner,Analyst,Diagnoser,Repairer,Synthesizer}}.\mathcal{R}=\left\{(r,P_{r})\;\middle|\;r\in\{\mathrm{Planner},\mathrm{Analyst},\mathrm{Diagnoser},\mathrm{Repairer},\mathrm{Synthesizer}\}\right\}.

These roles respectively construct equation search plans, extract evidence of observation, diagnose equation deficiencies, revise plans based on diagnoses, and integrate findings across branches. The ww controls the workflow structure. ℱ\mathcal{F} contains fixed tools and components shared by all candidates, including a base SR tool such as PySR (Cranmer, 2023) and an LLM-based equation generator, candidate management, and the final equation selector.

For each role rr, the full prompt includes runtime context, such as task information, search history, and feedback from other roles, together with two optimizable components Pr=(Ir,Er)P_{r}=(I_{r},E_{r}): an instruction IrI_{r} and a demonstration set ErE_{r}. The instruction IrI_{r} specifies the role’s objectives, reasoning requirements, and action principles. The demonstration set ErE_{r} illustrates the role’s task through input–output examples and may be empty. These components can alter the LLM’s reasoning strategies and outputs even with roles and workflows fixed.

We define the workflow using five discrete variables:

w=(uana,b,trep,tdis,usyn).w=\left(u_{\mathrm{ana}},b,t_{\mathrm{rep}},t_{\mathrm{dis}},u_{\mathrm{syn}}\right).

These variables jointly control role activation, parallel search, and iterative refinement, as summarized in Tab. 1.

The task-initiating Planner is always active and needs no control parameter. The Diagnoser–Repairer pair is active when trep>0t_{\mathrm{rep}}>0. Single-branch workflows omit cross-branch replanning and synthesis, requiring tdis=usyn=0t_{\mathrm{dis}}=u_{\mathrm{syn}}=0 when b=1b=1. Sec. 3.2 details the execution order and information flow.

We jointly optimize role instructions, demonstrations, and workflow organization on a training set 𝒟\mathcal{D} to maximize average equation quality under workflow-validity and execution-budget constraints:

(ℛ⋆,w⋆)∈arg⁡maxℛ,ww∈𝒲B​J𝒟​(ℋ),where​J𝒟​(ℋ)=1|𝒟|​∑q∈𝒟Q⁡(S⁡(q),q).(\mathcal{R}^{\star},w^{\star})\in\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{R},\,w\\ w\in\mathcal{W}_{B}\end{subarray}}{\arg\max}\;J_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{H}),\ \text{where}\ J_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{H})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{D}}Q\!\left(S(q),q\right).

Here, 𝒲B\mathcal{W}_{B} contains workflows satisfying role dependencies and a per-task execution budget BB. Each candidate evaluation executes the complete solver and scores its final equation using the fixed quality score QQ. The stage-specific optimization sets 𝒟=∪{𝒟i}i=13\mathcal{D}=\cup\{\mathcal{D}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{3} and selection set 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva} are mutually disjoint random subsets of the public training set released by Xia et al. (2025). Each 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} is used for optimization in Stage ii, while 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva} is used for candidate selection during harness optimization. The three-stage optimization of HarnessSR approximately solves this objective to obtain the top-performing SR solver agent, and then applies it to new SR tasks.

3.2 Execution within an SR Agent Harness

Given task qq, the harness optionally invokes the Analyst to examine observations, then initializes bb branches. Each branch executes a Planner-generated plan using a base SR tool, followed by trept_{\mathrm{rep}} Diagnoser–Repairer refinement rounds. In each of the tdist_{\mathrm{dis}} cross-branch replanning rounds, each Planner uses a shared snapshot of preceding results to initiate another search. An optional Synthesizer produces one additional plan. Each role shares its prompt PrP_{r} across branches and rounds, while runtime context changes.

We integrate two selectable base SR algorithms as agent tools: PySR or an LLM-based equation generator, through a fixed, tool-specific adapter. For PySR, role outputs specify variable subsets, operator sets (unary_operators, binary_operators), structural restrictions (constraints, nested_constraints), and expression seeds (guesses) to constrain and seed evolutionary search. For the LLM-based generator, the adapter incorporates search guidance and structural hypotheses into the generation prompt and converts expression guesses into initial parameterized program skeletons. The generator retains its iterative equation-program generation, numerical parameter fitting, and evaluation procedures. For both tools, harness updates guide search through tool inputs while leaving the underlying algorithms unchanged.

Harness updates modify the parameters passed to the base SR algorithm. The shared components ℱ\mathcal{F} collect valid candidates and select the best equation f^q\hat{f}_{q}, which is scored by an external evaluator as QQ. Subsequent stages optimize prompts and workflows through this execution pipeline.

3.3 Stage 1: Role-Level Prompt Optimization

Stage 1 needs to identify a strong base prompt set for each single role, providing a starting point for the joint optimization of prompts and workflow in Stage 2. We optimize instructions IrI_{r} and demonstrations ErE_{r} of each role rr within simple workflows, retaining three high-scoring prompts per role for subsequent search and adaptation.

Optimization of Planner’ base prompts. We first fix the base workflow w=(0,1,0,0,0)w=(0,1,0,0,0), which structure is detailed in Tab. 2, and optimize the Planner’s instructions IPlannerI_{\rm Planner} and demonstrations EPlannerE_{\rm Planner}. By running the solver agent on 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, we extract input–output demonstrations from successful solver trajectories and use them, together with task information, to generate candidate instructions. Tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE) (Bergstra et al., 2011) searches over instruction–demonstration combinations, evaluating each through complete solver agent executions on 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva}. We retain the three highest-scoring combinations as the Planner’s base prompt packages for subsequent workflow search.

Optimization of other roles’ base prompts. With the Planner’s base prompt fixed, we optimize each remaining role within its corresponding workflow in Tab. 2, using the same prompt optimization procedure. Only the target roles’ instructions and demonstrations are updated; all other components remain fixed. Diagnoser and Repairer prompts are optimized and retained as paired configurations.

Prompt libraries. We remove duplicate and invalid versions, and retain the three highest-scoring prompts per role. Diagnoser and Repairer prompts remain paired, yielding four libraries:

ℒr={Pr(1),Pr(2),Pr(3)},r∈{Planner,Analyst,DiagRepair,Synthesizer}.\mathcal{L}_{r}=\{P_{r}^{(1)},P_{r}^{(2)},P_{r}^{(3)}\},\quad r\in\{\mathrm{Planner},\mathrm{Analyst},\mathrm{DiagRepair},\mathrm{Synthesizer}\}.

Each package contains one Pr=(Ir,Er)P_{r}=(I_{r},E_{r}), or a paired diagnosis–repair configuration.

These prompts are initial candidates rather than final configurations. Stage 2 jointly optimizes both workflow and prompts, while Stage 3 further refines the instructions using SR execution feedback for task adaptation.

3.4 Stage 2: Joint Workflow and Prompt Optimization

Stage 2 jointly searches workflows and prompt assignments, then briefly adapts the selected prompts to their workflows before choosing candidates for Stage 3.

Candidate agent initialization. We initialize each agent candidate by sampling a workflow and then assigning prompts to it.

Firstly, we construct workflow space 𝒲B\mathcal{W}_{B} by enumerating the parameter combinations in Tab. 1 and removing those that violate role dependencies or execution-budget constraints. We select nn distinct workflows from 𝒲B\mathcal{W}_{B}, which include six basic workflows (the four listed in Tab. 2, two-branch independent search (0,2,0,0,0)(0,2,0,0,0), and cross-branch replanning (0,2,0,1,0)(0,2,0,1,0), illustrated in Fig. 2). The remaining workflows are sampled uniformly without replacement from 𝒲B\mathcal{W}_{B}.

Secondly, for each sampled workflow, we assign a prompt to every role by probabilistic sampling from the corresponding Stage 1 library: higher-scoring packages are more likely to be selected, while lower-scoring ones remain available for exploration. We repeat this assignment twice for each workflow, resampling duplicate assignments, to obtain 2​n2n initial harnesses.

We represent each candidate agent by (w,z)(w,z), where ww specifies the workflow and z=(zPlanner,zAnalyst,zDiagRepair,zSynthesizer)z=\left(z_{\mathrm{Planner}},z_{\mathrm{Analyst}},z_{\mathrm{DiagRepair}},z_{\mathrm{Synthesizer}}\right) specifies its prompt assignment. Each zr∈{1,2,3}z_{r}\in\{1,2,3\} selects package Pr(zr)P_{r}^{(z_{r})} from ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r}, determining the corresponding role prompts PrP_{r} in ℛ\mathcal{R}. Only indices for active role groups are used; Diagnoser and Repairer share one package index.

Joint search with TPE. We use the TPE (Bergstra et al., 2011) to optimize (w,z)(w,z): the five workflow parameters in ww and up to four active prompt-package indices in zz. We first evaluate the 2​n2n initial harnesses on 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} and initialize TPE with their configurations and scores. At each iteration, TPE divides evaluated configurations into high-scoring candidates and the remainder, models their parameter distributions, and proposes a new (w,z)(w,z) favored by the high-scoring distribution relative to the other. The resulting solver is evaluated on the same panel, and its score updates the search history. This loop can change both workflow structure and prompt assignment across the full valid space. Therefore, during TPE search, the prompts obtained in Stage 1 remain fixed and are only reassigned across different workflows. Invalid or previously evaluated configurations are excluded.

Brief prompt adaptation for top candidates. TPE can only search for better prompt–workflow combinations within a fixed space and cannot generate new prompts. Because prompts and workflows are tightly coupled, Stage 1 prompts may become suboptimal for the workflows found in Stage 2 and bias their evaluation. We therefore briefly refine the each role’s instruction IrI_{r} of promising candidates before allocating the larger Stage 3 optimization budget.

We select the best KK candidate agents with different workflows based on joint search and fix their workflows and demonstrations. For every role of each top candidate, we ask an LLM to propose a small set of instruction variants informed by role input, output, and execution feedback. TPE then searches for combinations of these variants, evaluating each combination through complete solver executions on a small subset of 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}. Finally, we retain the best instruction combination for each top candidate, effectively fine-tuning its prompts.

3.5 Stage 3: SR-Guided Instruction Refinement

Brief adaptation improves prompt–workflow compatibility but cannot fully address persistent failures in equation search. Stage 3 therefore refines the KK Stage 2 candidates using SR-specific execution feedback. For each candidate, we fix the workflow ww, demonstrations ErE_{r}, and shared components ℱ\mathcal{F}, and optimize only the role instructions IrI_{r} to better adapt them to SR tasks.

SR diagnostic feedback. Each workflow maintains a separate candidate pool 𝒞w\mathcal{C}_{w}, initialized with its adapted harness from Stage 2. At each iteration, we uniformly sample a parent ℋw\mathcal{H}_{w} from the pool and execute it on 𝒟3\mathcal{D}_{3}, recording every role’s input and output, search plans, candidate equations, and observational residuals.

An external diagnostic LLM examines these traces and reports identified problems, supporting evidence, and affected roles. It checks and constructs four types of diagnostic feedback: (i) evidence-to-action alignment, checking whether residual patterns and diagnoses lead to concrete search-plan changes; (ii) structural exploration, examining whether branches and rounds explore distinct equation forms and improve candidate quality; (iii) constraint justification, identifying variable, operator, or structural restrictions unsupported by available evidence; and (iv) expression quality, examining fit, complexity, and numerical validity to inform subsequent planning.

This step diagnoses behavior without rewriting instructions or accessing reference equations, ensuring that the diagnostics are not tailored to specific training problems.

Feedback-guided instruction revision. The reflection model (Agrawal et al., 2026) receives the active roles’ current instructions and the diagnostic feedback, proposes evidence-supported changes, and produces revised instructions for every roles of candidate workflow. The resulting prompts form a child harness ℋw′=(ℛ′={(r,Pr′)},w,ℱ)\mathcal{H}_{w}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}=\{(r,P^{\prime}_{r})\},w,\mathcal{F}).

Determining the Final SR Harness. Parent and child are evaluated on 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva}. The child enters 𝒞w\mathcal{C}_{w} only if

J𝒟eva​(ℋ′)>J𝒟eva​(ℋ).J_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva}}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime})>J_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm eva}}(\mathcal{H}).

Otherwise, it is discarded. We repeat this process until the optimization budget is exhausted.

We evaluate the candidates in each pool on 𝒟3\mathcal{D}_{3} and retain the highest-scoring harness for each of the KK workflows. We then evaluate these KK harnesses on 𝒟3∪𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{3}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eva}} and select the top-performing one as the final SR agent harness.

4 Experiments

We evaluate HarnessSR’s accuracy and efficiency, compare harness optimization with model-weight post-training, and analyze the contributions of optimization stages, workflow search, and diagnostic feedback. The appendices provide experimental configurations and role instructions (C–E and G), alongside optimization costs ( A), symbolic accuracy (B), alternative SR backend comparisons (E), out-of-distribution results (F), equation-recovery cases (H), and training-set-size analysis (I).

4.1 Experimental setup

Data.

Following SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025), we evaluate on LSR-Synth, the synthetic subset of LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b), comprising 129 tasks across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Harness optimization uses the 1,024 public synthetic training tasks released by SR-Scientist. The effect of training-set size is examined in Appendix I. Dataset details are provided in Appendix C.1.

Models and baselines.

We use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B supports the main results and ablations; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct supports the comparison with model-weight post-training; and GPT-OSS-20B tests applicability to another model family with fewer total parameters. The non-LLM baselines are GPLearn, E2E, NeSymReS, DSR, uDSR, and PySR. The LLM-based baselines are LaSR, LLM-SR, and SR-Scientist; SR-Scientist+RL is used for the post-training comparison. Model and search settings are given in Appendices C and E; baseline settings are in Appendix D.

Metrics.

Following LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b) and SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025), we use accuracy-to-tolerance, Accτ\mathrm{Acc}_{\tau}. For each task, we discard the 5% of test points with the largest relative errors and check whether all remaining errors are at most τ\tau. We report the proportion of tasks meeting this criterion at τ=0.01\tau=0.01 and 0.0010.001, together with mean solving time per task. Evaluation and timing details are provided in Appendices C.2 and C.3. We measure optimization effort by the total number of solver executions. Each execution is one run of an SR solver on one task and may include multiple LLM and SR-tool calls; repeated runs on the same task are counted separately. Symbolic-equivalence accuracy (SA) and supplementary OOD results are reported in Appendices B and F, respectively.

4.2 Main results

Table 3 shows that HarnessSR’s mean ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} and Acc0.001\mathrm{Acc}_{0.001} across the three backbones are 45.0% and 63.8% higher than those of the next-best baseline, SR-Scientist, respectively. Mean solving time is reduced by 58.0–85.7% relative to the fastest LLM-based baseline in each model group. Joint prompt–workflow optimization and SR-guided instruction refinement help translate solving feedback into more effective equation search.

These gains extend across scientific domains. HarnessSR leads at both accuracy thresholds in all four domains with the two Qwen models, and in physics, biology, and materials science with GPT-OSS-20B.

4.3 Comparison with reinforcement-learning post-training

Table 4 compares weight post-training and harness optimization using the same Qwen3-Coder base model. HarnessSR achieves 57.36% ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01}, compared with 40.92% for SR-Scientist+RL, and also leads at ID Acc0.001\mathrm{Acc}_{0.001}. HarnessSR keeps model weights fixed and improves guidance for SR tools by optimizing role search instructions and their interactions. This result supports harness optimization as an effective route to improving symbolic regression performance. The one-time investments for both optimization routes are given in Appendix A.

4.4 LLM calls versus accuracy

Figure 3 compares accuracy and LLM calls using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. HarnessSR achieves the highest accuracy at both thresholds with an average of 23 calls per task, about 6.2% of the call count at SR-Scientist’s final point. SR-Scientist, LLM-SR, and LaSR improve as calls accumulate, but their final accuracies remain below HarnessSR despite hundreds or up to a thousand calls. One-time optimization determines role search instructions, branch organization, and interaction rounds; the resulting configuration is then used directly on new tasks. The figure shows that reusing this configuration achieves higher accuracy with fewer model calls.

4.5 Contribution of optimization stages

Table 5 shows that all three optimization stages improve accuracy. Stage 1 optimizes role prompts within basic workflows, establishing a useful starting point for the full solver. Stage 2 jointly searches workflows and prompt assignments, then briefly adapts role instructions to the selected workflows so that prompts fit their role combinations and interactions. ID Acc0.001\mathrm{Acc}_{0.001} rises from 16.54% to 32.82%.

Stage 3 raises ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} from 43.41% to 65.37% and ID Acc0.001\mathrm{Acc}_{0.001} from 32.82% to 38.76%. SR diagnostics connect candidate equations, residual patterns, and role actions, checking whether solving feedback leads to changes in search plans and whether different branches explore distinct equation structures. The reflection model uses these diagnostics to revise role instructions, improving guidance for subsequent equation search while keeping the workflow fixed.

4.6 Workflow search and diagnostic feedback

Table 6 shows that SR diagnostics improve accuracy at both thresholds under both search strategies, with larger gains in full-space search. The diagnostics connect candidate-equation structures and residual patterns with role actions, giving instruction revision concrete directions for equation search. This feedback guides role-prompt optimization more effectively than using execution traces directly, including when more workflows are available. Combining full-space search with SR diagnostics raises ID Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} from 49.35% to 65.37% and reduces mean LLM calls per task from 37 to 23, compared with fixed-pool search using execution traces.

5 Conclusion and Limitation

We introduced HarnessSR, a framework that treats the SR agent harness itself as an optimization target. It jointly optimizes role instructions, demonstrations, and workflow organization while keeping model weights and underlying search algorithms fixed. Results on LSR-Synth support this approach as a way to construct stronger, reusable SR agents. A central implication for SR is that numerical feedback can inform both equation refinement within a task and the development of search strategies reused across tasks. Through harness optimization, evidence from training tasks shapes how agents propose hypotheses, interpret residuals, and organize exploration and refinement on new problems. Prompts and workflows therefore encode consequential choices about how equation discovery proceeds. This perspective motivates studying solver organization as an optimization dimension in SR, alongside equation representations and search algorithms.

However, the present formulation searches within a predefined workflow space. Whether more open-ended workflow structures can reveal additional reusable strategies for equation discovery remains an important question for future research.

Appendix A One-time Optimization Cost

The main text compares two adaptation routes on the same Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct base model: SR-Scientist+RL updates model weights through reinforcement learning, whereas HarnessSR keeps the weights fixed and searches reusable role prompts and solver workflows. Table 7 reports the one-time investment required to obtain each final solver; the training task counts and solver execution counts refer to the optimization stage.

Because of computational constraints, we did not reproduce the reinforcement learning training of SR-Scientist. Its evaluation results, training configuration, and model information are taken from the original paper, official code repository, and Hugging Face model page (Xia et al., 2025). Its 15,360 trajectories follow from 60 training steps, 32 prompts per step, and eight samples per prompt. Each sampled task-level trajectory counts as one solver execution in Table 7. We deploy vLLM on two H100 GPUs to serve concurrent model requests during Harness search.

Appendix B Symbolic Accuracy

Following the evaluation method of SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025), we use GPT-OSS-120B to assess the symbolic equivalence of predicted and ground-truth equations and report symbolic accuracy (SA).

Appendix C Data, Evaluation, and Model Settings

C.1 Training Tasks and Scientific Domains

LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b) comprises LSR-Synth and LSR-Transform. LSR-Synth combines terms from established scientific equations with newly constructed terms, whereas LSR-Transform modifies existing equations. Following SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025), we use LSR-Synth because transformed equations may retain clues encountered during model pretraining. Each task provides observed data and separate in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test points.

Harness optimization uses a pool of 1,024 public synthetic training tasks released with SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025). The training-scale comparison uses 80, 160, 320, and 640 tasks. Training tasks provide role demonstrations, assess candidate prompts and workflows, and supply solver feedback for instruction revision. The final solver harness is frozen before evaluation on the 129 official LSR-Synth tasks.

LSR-Synth spans physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Table 9 summarizes representative tasks, input variables, and prediction targets in the four domains, following the examples in LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b).

C.2 Locked-Equation Evaluation and Aggregation

Each method outputs one locked equation per task. The external evaluator computes its predictions on separate in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test points; the solver receives observed data, variable descriptions, and scientific context. We use accuracy-to-tolerance, Accτ\mathrm{Acc}_{\tau}, following LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b) and SR-Scientist (Xia et al., 2025). For either distribution, let task qq have nqn_{q} test points, with target yq,iy_{q,i} and locked-equation prediction y^q,i\hat{y}_{q,i} at point ii. For nonzero targets, the relative error is

eq,i=|y^q,i−yq,i||yq,i|.e_{q,i}=\frac{|\hat{y}_{q,i}-y_{q,i}|}{|y_{q,i}|}. (1)

Sort the relative errors and discard the largest ⌊0.05​nq⌋\lfloor 0.05n_{q}\rfloor. Let ℐq\mathcal{I}_{q} index the remaining test points. At threshold τ∈{0.01,0.001}\tau\in\{0.01,0.001\}, the task-level indicator is

aq,τ=[maxi∈ℐqeq,i≤τ],a_{q,\tau}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{q}}e_{q,i}\leq\tau\right], (2)

where 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] equals one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. For a set of NN tasks, accuracy in percent is

Accτ=100N​∑q=1Naq,τ.\mathrm{Acc}_{\tau}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{q=1}^{N}a_{q,\tau}. (3)

For domain dd with ndn_{d} tasks, write Ad,τ=100​∑q∈daq,τ/ndA_{d,\tau}=100\sum_{q\in d}a_{q,\tau}/n_{d}. Overall accuracy weights domains by their task counts:

Accτ=44​Aphysics,τ+36​Achemistry,τ+24​Abiology,τ+25​Amaterials,τ129.\mathrm{Acc}_{\tau}=\frac{44A_{\mathrm{physics},\tau}+36A_{\mathrm{chemistry},\tau}+24A_{\mathrm{biology},\tau}+25A_{\mathrm{materials},\tau}}{129}. (4)

ID and OOD evaluation use the same locked equation and numerical criterion, with test points drawn from different input distributions.

C.3 Base Models and Per-Task Time

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is used for the main results and method ablations. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct supports the comparison with SR-Scientist+RL, which is post-trained from the same base model. GPT-OSS-20B shows the method’s performance on another model family. For each base model, Harness optimization modifies role prompts and workflows while holding model weights fixed. The per-task Harness budget is at most 40 role-model calls and 24 symbolic regression (SR) backend calls. Both Qwen models are served through vLLM; the solver roles use LLM sampling temperature 0.7, while comparison methods follow their respective public decoding configurations.

Mean per-task time is measured from the start of solving a task to the locking of its final equation, including model calls and SR backend solving, and averaged over evaluation tasks. This metric measures the per-task running time of the optimized solver; the one-time Harness optimization cost is reported in Appendix A.

For each base model, LaSR, LLM-SR, SR-Scientist, and HarnessSR are timed sequentially with exclusive use of the same GPU inference resources and serving configuration. The inference service uses vLLM 0.29.0, with six A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs allocated to each base model and two AMD EPYC 9654 CPUs. Each GPU hosts an independent inference instance, with a per-instance concurrent request limit of 64. For Qwen3-Coder, this limit is 27 due to key-value (KV) cache capacity constraints, and remains the same across methods using this model. Each method retains its own parallelism: LaSR issues up to 10 concurrent requests per task, and LLM-SR samples four candidates in parallel per prompt.

To check for resource contention during timing, we record running and queued request counts, KV cache occupancy, and CPU usage every 30 seconds. In the monitored samples, running request counts remain below the per-instance concurrency limits, no sustained queues are observed, and KV cache occupancy does not exceed 10%. CPU utilization of the baseline jobs and the HarnessSR control process, normalized by their allocated core counts, does not exceed 60%.

C.4 Harness Optimization Settings

The main experiment uses 160 training tasks divided into four mutually disjoint sets: 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}, and 𝒟3\mathcal{D}_{3} each contain 32 tasks, and 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eva}} contains 64 tasks. Stage ii uses 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} for optimization, while 𝒟eva\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eva}} is used for candidate selection.

Stage 1 performs six TPE configuration evaluations per role group. Stage 2 initializes n=8n=8 workflows, comprising six basic configurations and two sampled configurations. Two prompt assignments per workflow produce 16 initial harnesses. TPE evaluates eight additional configurations, for 24 configurations in total. The top K=6K=6 candidates undergo brief adaptation on an eight-task subset of 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}, with two TPE configuration evaluations per candidate.

Stage 3 performs at most four instruction-refinement rounds for each of these six candidates. Prompt-bundle construction, candidate acceptance, and final selection follow the procedures in Section 3.

Appendix D Comparison Methods

The comparison methods span evolutionary search, neural-symbolic generation, LLM-assisted search, and autonomous tool interaction. We describe the mechanisms and experimental configurations of the ten baselines below.

GPLearn.

GPLearn evolves expression trees with genetic programming, improving fit across generations through selection, crossover, and mutation (Stephens, 2024). The gplearn SymbolicRegressor uses 500 individuals, 200 generations, and tournament size 20. Its functions are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, sine, cosine, square root, logarithm, absolute value, negation, and reciprocal. It provides a conventional evolutionary baseline without a pretrained model or LLM inference.

E2E.

E2E uses a pretrained Transformer to predict equation structure and constants directly from observations, followed by numerical refinement (Kamienny et al., 2022). We use the public facebookresearch/symbolicregression implementation, at most 200 observed points per task, and refinement of 10 candidate expression trees. It tests whether pretrained end-to-end structure prediction can recover these new synthetic equations.

NeSymReS.

NeSymReS encodes observed points, generates symbolic expressions, and fits constants in candidate structures (Biggio et al., 2021). The public NeuralSymbolicRegressionThatScales implementation receives 500 points per task and uses beam width 32. It represents a neural generation approach with a distinct candidate search procedure from E2E.

DSR.

DSR samples expressions symbol by symbol with a recurrent neural network and uses risk-seeking policy gradients to increase the probability of high-scoring expressions (Petersen et al., 2021). The deep-symbolic-optimization implementation samples up to 100,000 expressions per task, with batch size 512 and learning rate 0.0005. Expression length ranges from 1 to 9; operators are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, sine, cosine, exponential, and logarithm. Its task-specific learned search provides a direct reference for uDSR.

uDSR.

uDSR adds genetic programming and a polynomial poly operator to neural-guided expression search (Landajuela et al., 2022). Neural search retains DSR’s sample budget, batch size, and learning rate. The genetic population is 100, run for 20 generations, with crossover and mutation probabilities of 0.5, tournament size 5, and maximum mutation-tree depth 3. Its operator set adds poly to DSR’s operators. This comparison shows the effect of combining search mechanisms.

PySR.

PySR searches equations through multiple evolutionary populations and maintains a trade-off between fit and expression complexity (Cranmer, 2023). The independent baseline runs one backend solve per task with all input variables and operators: 125 iterations, 550 cycles per iteration, 15 populations of size 33, maximum expression size 40, and randomization weight 0.1. Binary operators are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and power; unary operators are exponential, logarithm, square root, sine, and cosine. Its final equation selection rule is given in Appendix E.1. This baseline uses the same class of SR backend as HarnessSR, making the contribution of role guidance and workflow coordination visible.

LaSR.

LaSR maintains an LLM-proposed natural-language concept library within evolutionary equation search and uses those concepts to generate and modify equations (Grayeli et al., 2024). We use LibraryAugmentedSymbolicRegression.jl: 25 iterations, 550 cycles each, 10 populations of size 33, maximum expression size 30, and the concept library enabled. The LLM operation weights for mutation, crossover, and random generation are all 0.001. Operators and nesting constraints match the independent PySR baseline. The response limit is 4,096 tokens, with up to 1,000 model requests per task.

LLM-SR.

LLM-SR represents equations as programs, uses scientific context and strong existing candidates to propose new programs, and advances the search through execution and constant fitting (Shojaee et al., 2025a). We use the baseline configuration released with LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b), allowing at most 1,000 model calls per task. Each prompt samples four independent candidates, with one call counted per candidate. The method’s candidate selector determines the final equation and selects from candidates available at each call checkpoint in Figure 3.

SR-Scientist.

SR-Scientist uses an LLM to call data-analysis and equation-evaluation tools, revises hypotheses from observed feedback, and carries a cache of previous strong equations across iterations (Xia et al., 2025). We use the public inference framework, with at most 40 iterations and 25 interaction rounds per iteration; the cache provides the top three equations to the next iteration. Temperature is 0.7, top_p=1.0, the response limit is 8,192 tokens, and the initial mean absolute percentage error target is 0.1%. The evaluator fits constants with BFGS. Its public candidate selection rule determines the final equation. Iterations, interaction rounds, and the cache govern different steps; Figure 3 uses actual call counts to describe its inference demand.

SR-Scientist+RL.

This variant post-trains Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct through reinforcement learning and retains SR-Scientist’s inference-time tool workflow. We use the released GAIR/SR-Scientist-30B model (Xia et al., 2025); its one-time training investment is given in Appendix A. It compares model-weight updates with Harness optimization in final solving performance.

D.1 Call-Accuracy Trajectories

Figure 3 uses the same 129 evaluation tasks. The twelve LLM-SR checkpoints take the first 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 40, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800, or 1,000 LLM calls for each task. Its original selection rule based on observed data locks the equation available by that checkpoint. Table 10 reports each point’s accuracy. The checkpoint call count is the actual cumulative calls made by the method on each task.

At the end of SR-Scientist iteration rr, its selection rule based on observed data chooses one equation from each task’s candidates through that iteration. Tasks that end early retain their final equation and cumulative call count in later iterations. The horizontal coordinate is the mean of cumulative calls on the 129 tasks, xr=129−1​∑q=1129cq,rx_{r}=129^{-1}\sum_{q=1}^{129}c_{q,r}, where cq,rc_{q,r} is the number of calls actually made for task qq through iteration rr; the vertical coordinate is overall accuracy at that iteration. Table 11 lists iterations 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40. The HarnessSR point is the aggregate after the frozen solver completes on the same task set.

LaSR checkpoint rr takes the candidates after the 10​r10r-th population return for each task, r=1,…,25r=1,\ldots,25. Figure 3 plots all 25 rounds and a separately locked run-completion point. Each checkpoint uses LaSR’s selection rule based on observed data before evaluation by the same external evaluator. The horizontal coordinate averages the actual cumulative LLM calls over 129 tasks, and the vertical coordinate uses all 129 tasks as its denominator. Table 12 reports rounds 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25, and run completion. Model calls continue after round 25, so the final cumulative count is slightly higher while accuracy is unchanged.

Appendix E Symbolic Regression Backends and Candidate Selection

With continued advances in the field, symbolic regression (SR) has attracted increasing attention (Chen et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Meidani et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2023b; Kamienny et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025; Shojaee et al., 2025a). Beyond numerical prediction, SR transforms observations into testable scientific hypotheses, enabling equation discovery across physics, biology, materials science, and other domains (Yu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023a; Hu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024). Among the diverse families of SR methods, we select two representative approaches—a GP-based solver and an LLM-based solver—as the base SR tools in HarnessSR. By covering fundamentally different search paradigms, this choice demonstrates that HarnessSR can integrate heterogeneous SR algorithms as underlying tools rather than being restricted to a specific class of solvers.

We compare three SR backends: PySR, LLM equation generation, and a hybrid of LLM and PySR. For each backend, we independently run all three stages of harness optimization to search for its role prompts and solver workflow. Each resulting harness is then frozen for evaluation.

E.1 PySR Backend

The main experiments use the PySR backend, with the same base settings as the independent PySR baseline in Appendix D. Roles can specify subsets of input variables and operators, structural constraints, and initial expressions; the adapter maps this guidance into PySR search settings. The independent PySR baseline runs one backend solve with the full variable and operator sets.

The selector computes candidate relative root mean square error on observed points with nonzero targets. Let e∗e^{*} be the lowest error. It first retains candidates with error no greater than e∗+max⁡(0.05​e∗,10−4)e^{*}+\max(0.05e^{*},10^{-4}) and then chooses the expression with the fewest nodes. Thus, when fits are close, the simpler expression is preferred. HarnessSR and the independent PySR baseline use this same final selection rule.

E.2 LLM Equation-Generation Backend

For an LLM equation generator, the adapter includes search guidance and structural hypotheses in the equation-generation prompt and turns expression guesses into initial program skeletons with free parameters. The generator then creates candidates, fits constants, and evaluates them. This backend draws on LLM-SR’s equation-program generation and constant fitting (Shojaee et al., 2025a), and on SR-Scientist’s use of execution feedback to improve candidates (Xia et al., 2025). Its input includes scientific context, variable descriptions, a summary of observed data, and the roles’ structural hypotheses, analysis, and repair directions. The equation generator and solver roles use the same base model. Its role prompts and solver workflow are obtained through independent harness optimization with the LLM equation-generation backend.

One backend call consists of two rounds of generation and evaluation. Following LLM-SR’s sampling design, each round independently samples eight responses, and each response may provide up to ten candidate programs; one backend call therefore makes at most sixteen generation requests. Candidate programs are parsed, checked for numerical validity, and deduplicated by equation skeleton. Free constants are fitted with Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least squares from up to 32 starting points. Fitted candidates are scored on observed data; stronger equations and their scores are retained as generation experience. The second round uses the first round’s fitting feedback to generate and evaluate further candidates. Equations and evaluations from both rounds are returned to the Harness for subsequent diagnosis, repair, and final equation selection.

E.3 Hybrid Backend

The hybrid configuration independently searches for its own role prompts and solver workflow. For a given problem, it executes complete solves with the LLM equation-generation backend and the PySR backend, pools the candidates from both routes, and selects one final equation. Both the LLM-only and hybrid configurations evaluate candidates using the 95th percentile of relative error on observed points, together with expression complexity and numerical validity; simpler expressions are preferred when errors are close. The merge makes no further LLM calls or constant fits.

Table 13 shows that the hybrid configuration achieves higher accuracy than the LLM-only configuration and slightly exceeds the PySR configuration used in the main experiments. These results support the applicability of harness optimization to different equation-search backends.

Appendix F Out-of-Distribution Results

Figures 4–6 compare ID and OOD accuracy by base model; Table 14 reports the OOD results.

On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, HarnessSR reaches 61.24% OOD Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01}, above LLM-SR (34.88%) and SR-Scientist (44.19%) on the same base model. Across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science, its accuracy is 53.79%, 50.93%, 61.11%, and 89.33%, compared with 31.82%, 25.00%, 50.00%, and 88.00% for SR-Scientist. On Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, HarnessSR reaches 55.04% overall, with 37.88%, 43.52%, 62.50%, and 94.67% across the four domains.

Compared with the main-text ID results, HarnessSR changes from 65.37% to 61.24% OOD Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} on Qwen3.6, a difference of 4.13 percentage points; on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct it changes from 57.36% to 55.04%, a difference of 2.32 points. HarnessSR reaches 59.69% OOD Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} on GPT-OSS-20B.

At each call, task context, observations, and search state are supplied as runtime input; the symbolic regression (SR) backend executes the search plans. References to PySR in the original instructions are retained.

G.2 Final PySR Solver Workflow and Role Instructions

This section presents the final solver workflow and role instructions used with the PySR backend in the main experiments. The solve begins with Analyst examining the task context, variables, and observed data. Three parallel search branches then run: in each branch, Planner prepares an initial plan and invokes the SR backend, followed by three rounds of Diagnoser diagnosis, Repairer plan revision, and backend solving. Synthesizer collects candidate equations across branches, proposes an additional plan, and runs the backend once more. All candidates from initial search, repair, and synthesis are evaluated and selected together to produce the final equation. Full execution uses 23 role-model calls and 13 SR-backend calls.

Appendix H Successful Equation-Recovery Cases

We select three successful cases involving population growth, a nonlinear oscillator, and material stress to show the recovered equation structures and their ID and OOD predictions. ID and OOD denote the two test distributions, and NMSE is normalized mean squared error. A “Pass” in Table 15 means that the task meets the indicated accuracy threshold on that distribution. Each case has 500 ID and 500 OOD points.

H.1 Population Growth: BPG10

This task takes time tt and population size PP as inputs and predicts the population growth rate. The ground truth and locked prediction are

d​Pd​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t} ≈0.1010081003​P0.3333333333+0.1010081003​P,\displaystyle\approx 0.1010081003\,P^{0.3333333333}+0.1010081003\,P, (5)
d​Pd​t^\displaystyle\widehat{\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}} =0.1010081​P0.3333332+0.1010081​P.\displaystyle=0.1010081\,P^{0.3333332}+0.1010081\,P. (6)

Both expressions combine a fractional-power term and a linear term under a shared coefficient; time does not appear explicitly in the final equation. At smaller PP, the P1/3P^{1/3} term is relatively more prominent, and its contribution relative to the linear term changes approximately as P−2/3P^{-2/3} as PP grows. The prediction preserves this joint nonlinear and linear dependence, with fitted exponent and coefficients close to the ground truth. The two predicted terms have the same coefficient at the recorded precision, matching the ground truth’s shared-coefficient form. ID and OOD NMSE are 2.9237×10−152.9237\times 10^{-15} and 4.5305×10−144.5305\times 10^{-14}, respectively, and the equation passes both accuracy thresholds on both sets of test points.

H.2 Nonlinear Oscillator: PO18

The inputs are position xx, time tt, and velocity vv; the target is the derivative of velocity. The ground truth combines a linear displacement-restoring term with nonlinear velocity coupling. The locked prediction retains the same variable combinations:

d​vd​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} =−ω02​x−β​v​sin⁡(x),\displaystyle=-\omega_{0}^{2}x-\beta v\sin(x), (7)
d​vd​t^\displaystyle\widehat{\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}} =−1.8126475​x−0.583656​v​sin⁡(x).\displaystyle=-1.8126475\,x-0.583656\,v\sin(x). (8)

The ground-truth β\beta and ω0\omega_{0} remain the dataset’s symbolic parameters, while the prediction gives fitted numerical coefficients. The xx term changes oppositely with position, and v​sin⁡(x)v\sin(x) couples velocity to position. Since sin⁡(x)\sin(x) changes sign, the direction of this coupling varies with position. Both terms vanish at x=0x=0; away from that point, position affects both the restoring term and the magnitude and direction of velocity coupling. The prediction adds no explicit time term and retains the ground truth’s concise dependence on state variables. ID and OOD NMSE are both below 2×10−152\times 10^{-15}, and the equation passes both thresholds.

H.3 Material Stress: MatSci22

This task predicts stress σ\sigma from strain ϵ\epsilon and temperature TT. The ground truth combines a quadratic strain term with a linear strain term that varies sinusoidally with temperature; the prediction uses cosine to express the same periodic family:

σ\displaystyle\sigma ≈72.33109008​ϵ2+7.74654609​ϵ​sin⁡(T−287.77390919),\displaystyle\approx 72.33109008\,\epsilon^{2}+7.74654609\,\epsilon\sin(T-287.77390919), (9)
σ^\displaystyle\hat{\sigma} =ϵ⁡[72.33109​ϵ−7.746545​cos⁡(T−3.4597688)].\displaystyle=\epsilon\bigl[72.33109\,\epsilon-7.746545\cos(T-3.4597688)\bigr]. (10)

Using −cos⁡z=sin⁡(z−π/2)-\cos z=\sin(z-\pi/2) and sine periodicity, the predicted periodic term can be written as 7.746545​ϵ​sin⁡(T−287.77390395)7.746545\,\epsilon\sin(T-287.77390395). Thus both expressions combine ϵ2\epsilon^{2} and ϵ​sin⁡(T−ϕ)\epsilon\sin(T-\phi). Their phases differ by approximately 5.24×10−65.24\times 10^{-6} radians, and the coefficients differ only slightly through numerical fitting. ID and OOD NMSE are 1.2594×10−111.2594\times 10^{-11} and 2.4181×10−102.4181\times 10^{-10}, respectively, with passes at both accuracy thresholds. The case shows how the same periodic structure can be expressed using sine or cosine and a phase shift.

Appendix I Effect of Training-Set Size

Table 16 shows that expanding the training set consistently improves the optimized solver’s accuracy. From 80 to 160 tasks, Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} rises from 52.71% to 65.37%, with improved accuracy at the stricter threshold as well. Accuracy continues to improve at 320 and 640 tasks, though each doubling brings a smaller gain. More training tasks provide richer solving feedback for role-prompt and workflow optimization, helping the resulting configuration recover equations on new tasks.

Further accuracy gains require greater one-time search effort. Relative to the main 160-task setting, 640 tasks entail about 3.45 times as many solver executions, raise Acc0.01\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01} from 65.37% to 69.51%, and further improve accuracy at the stricter threshold. The 160-task setting achieves substantial accuracy with moderate search effort, while larger training sets leave room for further gains. The results connect training scale, solver quality, and upfront search effort in harness optimization.
